text: You've now written real algorithms in both tools — Grover's, QFT, and teleportation in Q#, and the same family of algorithms in Qiskit from the earlier course in this path. This lesson asks the question directly: what is actually different about how these two tools think, not just how they're spelled?

Four things to take away: a Qiskit QuantumCircuit is data you build and inspect, while a Q# operation is itself the unit of computation. The operation-function split and compiler-derived functors buy you guarantees a dynamic circuit object can't give. Dynamic circuit objects buy you introspection and rewriting that a compiled, typed language doesn't give. And both tools express the same algorithms — the difference is the programming model, not raw capability.

In Qiskit, building a circuit means constructing a Python object and mutating it. qc is a real, inspectable object the whole time — you can print its gate list, draw it, count its depth, transpile it into a different gate set, or splice two circuits together. Nothing about building it requires running it; the circuit's existence as mutable, introspectable data is the entire point of the design.

In Q#, there's no equivalent intermediate object. PrepareBell isn't data describing a circuit — it's a compiled unit of computation. There's no dot-depth or dot-draw, because there's no runtime object sitting between the code you wrote and the computation actually happening. What you get instead is compiler-enforced structure: the operation-function split guarantees no hidden classical side effects masquerading as quantum logic, and the Adjoint and Controlled functors mean the compiler derives the inverse and controlled forms directly from the operation's declared structure.

Qiskit's object model makes circuit introspection and transformation a first-class, natural operation — transpilation, composition, visualization all fall directly out of the circuit being a Python object. The cost is that nothing guarantees a custom gate behaves correctly under its inverse or control methods — that's on you to verify. Q#'s typed model makes compiler-guaranteed correctness a first-class outcome — an operation that can't be adjointed is rejected at compile time, not discovered as a runtime surprise. The cost is you lose that ad hoc runtime circuit rewriting. Neither model is more capable; they fit different kinds of work.

Next lesson applies this same lens to a very concrete question both tools let you ask: how expensive is this program to run — and why Qiskit's tooling and Azure Quantum's resource estimator are answering genuinely different questions, not competing for the same answer.
